( [2025](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_WK_League "2025 WK League")) | | Most championships | [Incheon Hyundai Steel Red Angels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Incheon_Hyundai_Steel_Red_Angels "Incheon Hyundai Steel Red Angels")
(11 titles) | | Website | [kwff.or.kr](https://www.kwff.or.kr/wkleague) | | _Current: [2026 WK League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_WK_League "2026 WK League")_ | WK League The **WK League** ( [Hangul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hangul "Hangul"): WK리그) is a [semi-professional](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semi-professional_sports "Semi-professional sports") [women's football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_association_football "Women's association football") league,[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WK_League#cite_note-1)[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WK_League#cite_note-2) run by the [Korea Football Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korea_Football_Association "Korea Football Association") (KFA) and the [Korea Women's Football Federation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korea_Women's_Football_Federation "Korea Women's Football Federation") (KWFF), which represents the sport's highest level in South Korea.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WK_League#cite_note-3) [Icheon Daekyo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Icheon_Daekyo_WFC "Icheon Daekyo WFC") won the inaugural edition of the WK League in 2009 and won two more titles in 2011 and 2012. [Incheon Hyundai Steel Red Angels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Incheon_Hyundai_Steel_Red_Angels_WFC "Incheon Hyundai Steel Red Angels WFC") are the most successful team in the league, having won eleven consecutive titles between 2013 and 2023.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WK_League#cite_note-4) ## History \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=WK_League&action=edit§ion=1 "Edit section: History")\] ### Development and establishment of the league \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=WK_League&action=edit§ion=2 "Edit section: Development and establishment of the league")\] In 2006, the [Korea Women's Football Federation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korea_Women's_Football_Federation "Korea Women's Football Federation") (KWFF) announced their intention to start a semi-professional women's league the following year with four teams playing 12 to 15 games each across four or five rounds.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WK_League#cite_note-5) At the end of 2006 discussions were being held over player eligibility rules, in particular the issue of visas for foreign players.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WK_League#cite_note-6)[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WK_League#cite_note-:02-7) In January 2007, the KWFF clarified that the women's league would not be referred to as a professional league, and that official names under consideration included WK League, following the name of the men's [K League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K_League "K League") and adding a "W" to stand for "women's".[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WK_League#cite_note-:02-7) In 2008, the KWFF launched an exhibition league as a pilot for the planned year-round league, with four teams participating in three rounds, to be held alongside pre-existing football tournaments.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WK_League#cite_note-8) [Daekyo Kangaroos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Icheon_Daekyo_WFC "Icheon Daekyo WFC") won the exhibition league.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WK_League#cite_note-9) Following the pilot scheme, it was announced that the WK League would be launched in 2009.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WK_League#cite_note-:1-10) Due to the issue of securing stadiums in major cities, it was deemed too difficult to operate a home-and-away system. Instead, cities were selected to host a number of rounds each.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WK_League#cite_note-:1-10) The first edition of the league was contested by six teams over four rounds and 63 matches, including an all-star game and the championship final.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WK_League#cite_note-11) Matches were held on Monday nights to avoid clashes with other professional sports.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WK_League#cite_note-:2-12) ### Early years of the WK League (2009–2012) \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=WK_League&action=edit§ion=3 "Edit section: Early years of the WK League (2009–2012)")\] The first match of the [2009 WK League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2009_WK-League "2009 WK-League") took place on 20 April 2009 at Wolmyeong Sports Complex in [Gunsan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunsan "Gunsan") between Daekyo Kangaroos and [Hyundai Steel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Incheon_Hyundai_Steel_Red_Angels_WFC "Incheon Hyundai Steel Red Angels WFC"), resulting in a 0–0 draw.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WK_League#cite_note-13)[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WK_League#cite_note-14) Daekyo finished the regular season in first place and went on to win the championship final against Hyundai Steel to become the inaugural WK League champions.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WK_League#cite_note-15)[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WK_League#cite_note-16) In 2010, the South Korean government announced plans to invest in women's football, including the creation of two new clubs to compete in the WK League.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WK_League#cite_note-17) [Jeonbuk KSPO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hwacheon_KSPO_WFC "Hwacheon KSPO WFC") and [Chungbuk Sportstoto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sejong_Sportstoto_WFC "Sejong Sportstoto WFC") were both formally launched ahead of the [2011](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_WK-League "2011 WK-League") season, bringing the total number of teams in the league to eight.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WK_League#cite_note-18)[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WK_League#cite_note-19) However, the following year the league was reduced to seven teams following the dissolution of [Chungnam Ilhwa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chungnam_Ilhwa_Chunma_WFC "Chungnam Ilhwa Chunma WFC").[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WK_League#cite_note-20) From 2012 to 2016, the league continued with seven teams, meaning one team would sit out each round.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WK_League#cite_note-:4-21) [![A group of female football players, along with their managers, lift a large gold trophy, smiling joyfully.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7d/WK%EB%A6%AC%EA%B7%B8_2022.jpg/250px-WK%EB%A6%AC%EA%B7%B8_2022.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:WK%EB%A6%AC%EA%B7%B8_2022.jpg) Incheon Hyundai Steel Red Angels lift the WK League trophy in 2022 In 2013, the WK League drew the attention of local and international media following claims by six clubs that [Seoul WFC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seoul_WFC "Seoul WFC") striker [Park Eun-sun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Park_Eun-sun_(footballer) "Park Eun-sun (footballer)") was in fact a man.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WK_League#cite_note-22)[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WK_League#cite_note-23) It was reported that coaches from six teams threatened to boycott the [2014](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_WK_League "2014 WK League") league unless Park took a gender verification test.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WK_League#cite_note-24) Seoul WFC accused their rivals of violating Park's human rights and demanded an apology.[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WK_League#cite_note-25) Park also received support from an online petition as well as [Democratic Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_(South_Korea,_2013) "Democratic Party (South Korea, 2013)") politician Jun Byung-hun, who called for an investigation by the [National Human Rights Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Human_Rights_Commission_of_Korea "National Human Rights Commission of Korea").[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WK_League#cite_note-26) The six coaches involved claimed that the controversy was a private joke that had been leaked and blown out of proportion. Lee Sung-gyun of [Suwon FMC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suwon_FC_Women "Suwon FC Women") and [Yoo Dong-gwan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yoo_Dong-kwan "Yoo Dong-kwan") of [Goyang Daekyo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Icheon_Daekyo_WFC "Icheon Daekyo WFC") resigned in the aftermath of the row.[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WK_League#cite_note-27) In February 2014, the National Human Rights Commission advised the [Korea Football Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korea_Football_Association "Korea Football Association") (KFA) to punish the coaches, but neither the KFA nor the league itself handed down any punishment and as a result, Park eventually left Seoul to join [FC Rossiyanka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WFC_Rossiyanka "WFC Rossiyanka").[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WK_League#cite_note-28) ### Incheon dominance (2013–2023) \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=WK_League&action=edit§ion=4 "Edit section: Incheon dominance (2013–2023)")\] The 2013 season also saw Incheon Hyundai Steel Red Angels win their first WK League title, having finished as runners-up every year from 2009 to 2012.[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WK_League#cite_note-29) The club went on to win eleven consecutive titles.[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WK_League#cite_note-30) During this period of Incheon dominance, in [2015](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_WK_League "2015 WK League"), the league began a home-and-away system for the first time, allowing teams to establish stronger connections with regional governments and fanbases.[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WK_League#cite_note-31) [Gyeongju KHNP WFC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gyeongju_Korea_Hydro_&_Nuclear_Power_WFC "Gyeongju Korea Hydro & Nuclear Power WFC") joined the league in the [2017](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_WK_League "2017 WK League") season, bringing the total number of teams back to eight.[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WK_League#cite_note-32) At the end of the season, Icheon Daekyo ceased operations but was replaced in the WK League by new team [Changnyeong WFC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gangjin_Swans_WFC "Gangjin Swans WFC").[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WK_League#cite_note-33)[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WK_League#cite_note-34) ### Recent years (2024–present) \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=WK_League&action=edit§ion=5 "Edit section: Recent years (2024–present)")\] The Red Angels' run of WK League success came to an end in 2024, when the club finished in fourth place, outside of the playoff places for the first time in the history of the league.[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WK_League#cite_note-:3-35) Despite finishing second in the regular league, Suwon beat Hwacheon KSPO on aggregate in the championship final to lift the trophy for the second time, and the first time since the club merged with the [Suwon FC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suwon_FC "Suwon FC") men's team and rebranded as Suwon FC Women in 2022.[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WK_League#cite_note-36)[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WK_League#cite_note-:3-35) KSPO won their first title the following year, beating underdogs Seoul City in the championship final to become the first team in the history of South Korean women's football to complete a domestic [treble](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treble_(association_football) "Treble (association football)").[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WK_League#cite_note-37) Ahead of the 2026 season, Changnyeong WFC moved to [Gangjin County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gangjin_County "Gangjin County") in [South Jeolla Province](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Jeolla_Province "South Jeolla Province") and rebranded as Gangjin Swans WFC, becoming the region's first WK League side.[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WK_League#cite_note-38) ## Competition format \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=WK_League&action=edit§ion=6 "Edit section: Competition format")\] [![Teams and officials line up on a football pitch ready for a match.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fd/WK_League_playoff_at_Castle_Park.jpg/250px-WK_League_playoff_at_Castle_Park.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:WK_League_playoff_at_Castle_Park.jpg) The 2024 WK League play-off match between Suwon FC and Gyeongju KHNP, held at Suwon Sports Complex During the regular season, contested from March to September, each team plays a total of 28 games, playing four times against each of the other seven teams. Teams receive [three points for a win](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three_points_for_a_win "Three points for a win") and one point for a draw. No points are awarded for a loss. Teams are [ranked](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_tournament_ranking_system "Group tournament ranking system") by total points.[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WK_League#cite_note-:0-39) In the case that teams are level on points, tie-breakers are applied in the following order: 1. [Goal difference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goal_difference "Goal difference") 2. Head-to-head results 3. Total goals scored 4. Total wins 5. Drawing lots Then, the second and third-placed teams of the regular season face off in a one-legged play-off, with the winners facing the first-placed team of the regular season in a two-legged championship game. The remaining teams are ranked from fourth to eighth.[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WK_League#cite_note-:0-39) The regular season was reduced to 21 games in 2020 and 2021 due to the [COVID-19 pandemic in South Korea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic_in_South_Korea "COVID-19 pandemic in South Korea").[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WK_League#cite_note-40)[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WK_League#cite_note-41)[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WK_League#cite_note-42)[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WK_League#cite_note-43) A shortened season was maintained in 2022 due to the [2022 FIFA U-20 Women's World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_FIFA_U-20_Women's_World_Cup "2022 FIFA U-20 Women's World Cup") and the [2022 Asian Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Asian_Games "2022 Asian Games"), and again in 2023 due to the [2023 FIFA Women's World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_FIFA_Women's_World_Cup "2023 FIFA Women's World Cup").[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WK_League#cite_note-44)[\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WK_League#cite_note-45)[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WK_League#cite_note-46)[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WK_League#cite_note-47) The 2024 edition of the league saw a return to the 28-round regular season.[\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WK_League#cite_note-48)[\[49\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WK_League#cite_note-49) The WK League is the only women's league in the country and as such there is no relegation system in place. ## All-Star Game \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=WK_League&action=edit§ion=7 "Edit section: All-Star Game")\] The first all-star game was held on 10 August 2009, with players from all teams in the league competing as "Central All Stars" (players from Incheon Hyundai, Seoul WFC, and Suwon FMC) and "Southern All Stars" (players from Daekyo Kangaroos, Chunhnam Ilhwa, and Busan Sangmu).[\[50\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WK_League#cite_note-50) The game ended with a 3–2 victory for the Central All Stars. In 2010, following the same format, the Southern All Stars won 4–3.[\[51\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WK_League#cite_note-51) Following the expansion of the league in 2011, the all-star game was contested between "Team Gaia" (Goyang Daekyo, Busan Sangmu, Chungnam Ilhwa, Chungbuk Sportstoto) and "Team Athena" (Suwon FMC, Incheon Hyundai, Seoul WFC, Jeonbuk KSPO) and ended in a 9–6 win for Team Gaia, with six goals scored in the first half alone.[\[52\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WK_League#cite_note-52) In 2012, the format changed once again, with teams divided into two based on their position in the league following the 9th round of the regular season. While players were previously selected based on coaches' recommendations, for the first time fans were able to vote for coaches and players to participate.[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WK_League#cite_note-53) In an effort to promote the WK League and women's football more widely, the all-star game also featured attractions and gimmicks such as an autograph signing event, unique goal celebrations, celebrity guests, and a goalkeeper taking a penalty kick.[\[54\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WK_League#cite_note-54) The "Blue Mir" team (Goyang Daekyo, Jeonbuk KSPO, Chungnam Ilhwa, Suwon FMC) won 5–4 against the "Red Mir" team (Hyundai Steel, Seoul WFC, Chungbuk Sportstoto, Busan Sangmu).[\[55\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WK_League#cite_note-55) The 2013 all-star game saw a 4–4 draw between team "Phenomenon" (Hyundai Steel, Jeonbuk KSPO, Suwon FMC, Busan Sangmu) and team "Fantasy Star" (Goyang Daekyo, Chungbuk Sportstoto, Seoul WFC), with elaborate pre-rehearsed goal celebrations such as dancing to [Psy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psy "Psy")'s hit song " [Gentleman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gentleman_(Psy_song) "Gentleman (Psy song)")" and a portrayal of baseball player [Ryu Hyun-jin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyun-jin_Ryu "Hyun-jin Ryu")'s pitch.[\[56\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WK_League#cite_note-56)[\[57\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WK_League#cite_note-57) The 2014 all-star game was due to be held on 2 June, but was cancelled following the [sinking of the MV Sewol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sinking_of_MV_Sewol "Sinking of MV Sewol"), with the KWFF stating that it would not be appropriate to hold such a festive event during a period of national mourning.[\[58\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WK_League#cite_note-58) The event did not take place in 2015 due to South Korea's participation in the [2015 FIFA Women's World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_FIFA_Women's_World_Cup "2015 FIFA Women's World Cup").[\[59\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WK_League#cite_note-:5-59) When the all-star game returned to the schedule in 2016, it had a new format. Rather than an exhibition match between two all-star teams from within the league, a WK League all-stars team selected by a technical committee played against [1\. FFC Frankfurt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eintracht_Frankfurt_(women) "Eintracht Frankfurt (women)") in a friendly match held at [Ulsan Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulsan_Stadium "Ulsan Stadium").[\[59\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WK_League#cite_note-:5-59)[\[60\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WK_League#cite_note-60) The game finished as a 1–1 draw, and the WK League side won 5–3 in a [penalty shoot-out](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penalty_shoot-out_(association_football) "Penalty shoot-out (association football)").[\[61\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WK_League#cite_note-61) In 2017, the all-star game was held after the end of the league season in November rather than during the mid-season break. The WK League all-star team, selected by fan vote, hosted [INAC Kobe Leonessa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/INAC_Kobe_Leonessa "INAC Kobe Leonessa") at [Incheon Namdong Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Incheon_Namdong_Asiad_Rugby_Field "Incheon Namdong Asiad Rugby Field") in a match that resulted in a 2–2 draw. The WK League side won the subsequent penalty shoot-out 4–2.[\[62\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WK_League#cite_note-62)[\[63\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WK_League#cite_note-63) Following developments in inter-Korean relations, the KWFF hoped to invite a North Korean team for the 2018 all-star game, but an agreement could not be reached and the game was cancelled.[\[64\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WK_League#cite_note-:6-64)[\[65\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WK_League#cite_note-65) In 2019 and 2022, an all-star game was included in the league schedule with the date, location, and teams listed as "undecided".[\[66\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WK_League#cite_note-66)[\[67\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WK_League#cite_note-67) ## Clubs [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=WK_League&action=edit§ion=15 "Edit section: WK League draft")\] Each year the teams of the WK League participate in a draft to select new players from among graduating university students.[\[68\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WK_League#cite_note-69) Teams draw lots in the order of the previous year's final league position to determine the order of the draft.[\[69\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WK_League#cite_note-70) Drafted players' contract length and salary cap are determined by their position in the draft.[\[70\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WK_League#cite_note-71) Previously, draftees picked in the first four rounds of the draft signed '3+2' contracts, but these were changed to more basic three year contracts ahead of the 2026 season. The basic salaries for new draftees were also raised in 2026.[\[71\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WK_League#cite_note-72) | Round of draft | Contract length | Salary
(2026) | | --- | --- | --- | | 1 | 3 years | ₩34 million | | 2 | ₩32 million | | 3 | ₩30 million | | 4 | ₩26 million | | 5–10 | 1 year | ₩26 million | ### Military team recruitment \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=WK_League&action=edit§ion=16 "Edit section: Military team recruitment")\] The [Sangmu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korea_Armed_Forces_Athletic_Corps "Korea Armed Forces Athletic Corps") (military team) originally participated in the draft along with the other teams. All Sangmu players are required to join the military as a non-commissioned officer and undergo basic training for four months, leading to questions over the welfare of players drafted by the club.[\[72\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WK_League#cite_note-:03-73) The rules of the draft stated that if a player refused to join their drafted team, they were not permitted to sign to any team in the league for two years, making it difficult for rookie players to refuse to join the military if called up by Sangmu.[\[72\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WK_League#cite_note-:03-73) In 2014, South Korea international [Choe Yu-ri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Choe_Yu-ri "Choe Yu-ri") was selected by Busan Sangmu as their first pick in the draft. At first, Choe expressed concerns about joining the military and in particular not being able to train with the national squad during military training.[\[73\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WK_League#cite_note-74) She eventually refused to enter the military on the grounds that it infringed upon her freedom to choose a career.[\[74\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WK_League#cite_note-75) The incident led the KWFF to revise the rules of the draft, and Choe was selected by Daejeon Sportstoto in a special draft in 2015, after missing a season of league football.[\[75\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WK_League#cite_note-76)[\[76\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WK_League#cite_note-77) Since the 2016 season draft, rookie players can choose to apply to Sangmu, and the team selects their recruits from among the applicants. Applicants who are not selected are automatically included in the main draft. The Sangmu team is no longer permitted to participate in the draft.[\[77\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WK_League#cite_note-78) ### Foreign players \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=WK_League&action=edit§ion=17 "Edit section: Foreign players")\] When the league was established, each team was permitted to include two foreign players in their squad.[\[78\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WK_League#cite_note-:12-79) Daekyo Kangaroos became the first team to field a foreign player when they signed Brazilian striker [Pretinha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pretinha "Pretinha") in April 2009.[\[79\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WK_League#cite_note-80)[\[80\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WK_League#cite_note-81) ## Awards \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=WK_League&action=edit§ion=18 "Edit section: Awards")\] ### Official awards \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=WK_League&action=edit§ion=19 "Edit section: Official awards")\] The WK League Awards were first introduced by the Korea Women's Football Federation in 2022.[\[81\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WK_League#cite_note-:7-82) | Season | Most Valuable Player | Best new player | Best manager | Top goalscorer | Top assist provider | Best referee | Ref. | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | 2022 | —N/a[\[a\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WK_League#cite_note-83) | Kwon Hee-sun

team** ( [Korean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_language "Korean language"):대한민국 여자 축구 국가대표팀, recognised as **Korea Republic** by [FIFA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FIFA "FIFA")) represents [South Korea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Korea "South Korea") in international [women's football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_association_football "Women's association football") competitions. The South Korean women's team has qualified for five [FIFA World Cups](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FIFA_Women's_World_Cup "FIFA Women's World Cup") in 2003, 2015 (when they reached the round of 16), 2019, 2023 and 2027. ## History Main article: [History of the South Korea national football team](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_South_Korea_national_football_team "History of the South Korea national football team") ### Early history Further information: [Women's football in South Korea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_football_in_South_Korea "Women's football in South Korea") Less than a year after the government of the Republic of Korea was established in 1948, the first official women's football matches were held in [Seoul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seoul "Seoul") on 28 and 29 June 1949, as a part of the National Girls' and Women's Sport Games. While women's [basketball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_basketball "Women's basketball") and [volleyball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volleyball "Volleyball") won public recognition through the Games, football was seen as being unsuitable for women and unattractive to the public. As a result, the women's teams were disbanded soon after the event.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Korea_women's_national_football_team#cite_note-HongMangan2004-2) When women's football was officially adopted at the [1990 Asian Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1990_Asian_Games "1990 Asian Games") in [Beijing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beijing "Beijing"), the South Korean sports authorities decided to form a women's team with athletes from other sports and send the team to the Games.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Korea_women's_national_football_team#cite_note-HongMangan2004-2) The result was defeat in all matches against [Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan_women's_national_football_team "Japan women's national football team"), [North Korea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Korea_women's_national_football_team "North Korea women's national football team"), [China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_women's_national_football_team "China women's national football team") and [Chinese Taipei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Taipei_women's_national_football_team "Chinese Taipei women's national football team").[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Korea_women's_national_football_team#cite_note-3) Nevertheless, colleges and corporations started to launch women's football teams through the 1990s and the first annual national women's football event, the Queen's Cup, was held in 1993.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Korea_women's_national_football_team#cite_note-4) When the [1999 FIFA Women's World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_FIFA_Women's_World_Cup "1999 FIFA Women's World Cup") sparked interest worldwide, the South Korean ministry in charge of sports sponsored the foundation of new teams and tournaments for girls’ high school teams, university teams and company teams. To promote women's football, the Korea Women's Football Federation (KWFF) was established in March 2001, as an independent organization in association with the [Korea Football Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korea_Football_Association "Korea Football Association") (KFA).[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Korea_women's_national_football_team#cite_note-HongMangan2004-2) ### World Cup debut South Korea finished in third place at the [2003 AFC Women's Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2003_AFC_Women's_Championship "2003 AFC Women's Championship") and qualified for the [FIFA Women's World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FIFA_Women's_World_Cup "FIFA Women's World Cup") for the first time. The _Taegeuk Ladies_ were drawn in [Group B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2003_FIFA_Women's_World_Cup_Group_B "2003 FIFA Women's World Cup Group B") with [Norway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norway_women's_national_football_team "Norway women's national football team"), [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France_women's_national_football_team "France women's national football team") and [Brazil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazil_women's_national_football_team "Brazil women's national football team"). Their first match played at the World Cup was a 3–0 loss to Brazil. They then lost 1–0 to France and 7–1 to Norway,[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Korea_women's_national_football_team#cite_note-5) with [Kim Jin-hee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kim_Jin-hee_(footballer) "Kim Jin-hee (footballer)") scoring South Korea's first ever World Cup goal against the latter. They also won the inaugural [EAFF Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EAFF_E-1_Football_Championship_(women) "EAFF E-1 Football Championship (women)") on home soil in 2005.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Korea_women's_national_football_team#cite_note-6) The notable talents in South Korea appeared in the late 2000s. They won the [2009 Summer Universiade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Football_at_the_2009_Summer_Universiade_%E2%80%93_Women's_tournament "Football at the 2009 Summer Universiade – Women's tournament") and the [2010 FIFA U-17 Women's World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_FIFA_U-17_Women's_World_Cup "2010 FIFA U-17 Women's World Cup"), as well as finishing third at the [2010 FIFA U-20 Women's World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_FIFA_U-20_Women's_World_Cup "2010 FIFA U-20 Women's World Cup").[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Korea_women's_national_football_team#cite_note-7)[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Korea_women's_national_football_team#cite_note-8) The number of Women's World Cup berths in Asia was increased from three to five in 2012,[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Korea_women's_national_football_team#cite_note-9) which saw South Korea qualify for the [2015 FIFA Women's World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_FIFA_Women's_World_Cup "2015 FIFA Women's World Cup") as the fourth-placed team at the [2014 AFC Women's Asian Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_AFC_Women's_Asian_Cup "2014 AFC Women's Asian Cup").[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Korea_women's_national_football_team#cite_note-10) They earned their first ever World Cup victory by defeating [Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spain_women's_national_football_team "Spain women's national football team") 2–1 after a 2–0 loss to Brazil and a 2–2 draw with [Costa Rica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa_Rica_women's_national_football_team "Costa Rica women's national football team") in [Group E](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_FIFA_Women's_World_Cup_Group_E "2015 FIFA Women's World Cup Group E"). They made it out of the group stage for the first time with the new generation, although losing 3–0 to France in the [round of 16](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_FIFA_Women's_World_Cup_knockout_stage#Round_of_16 "2015 FIFA Women's World Cup knockout stage").[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Korea_women's_national_football_team#cite_note-11)[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Korea_women's_national_football_team#cite_note-12) ## Team image ### Nicknames The South Korea women's national football team has been known or nicknamed as the "Taegeuk Ladies" (태극낭자, _Taegeuk Nangja_). ### Kits and crest The women's team usually use exactly the same kit as its [male counterpart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Korea_national_football_team "South Korea national football team"), along with the combinations available, as of 2023. The two sides met for the first time in 1990, when South Korea suffered a 1–13 defeat at the hands of Japan. The South Korea women's team trailed behind Japan with just 4 wins, 11 draws and 18 losses as of 2022, in contrast to the fairly dominant performance of the [men's team](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Korea_national_football_team "South Korea national football team"). The reason for South Korea's weaker performance against Japan is that South Korea started to develop women's football much later than Japan. According to FIFA regulations, the principle is that a national team may play a maximum of two matches during the A match window. However, as the EAFF's request for FIFA approval was delayed, the current EAFF qualifying schedule does not meet the minimum 48-hour rest period required before matches to protect players. In the past, FIFA approved EAFF qualifying matches held in the same or similar manner without raising issues, but as FIFA has recently applied related regulations more strictly, this measure was taken. ## References 01.
